text.p: Opening arguments began on Wednesday in the O.J. Simpson civil trial with an attorney branding the former football star a "vengeful killer" and vowing to prove that he committed a brutal double-murder.

In an impassioned presentation to the jury, Daniel Petrocelli, a lawyer for the family of murder victim Ronald Goldman, contended that Goldman "died with his eyes open" and saw the man who killed him and his friend, Nicole Brown Simpson, O.J. Simpson's ex-wife.
"We will prove to you that Ronald Goldman and Nicole Brown Simpson died at the hands of the defendant, Orenthal James Simpson," Petrocelli told jurors in a crowded courtroom.
Simpson, who was acquitted of murder charges on Oct. 3, 1995, is now on trial in civil court in a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the victims' families.

Clad in a gray suit and red tie, Simpson sat just behind his defence attorneys as the trial moved into high gear after a month of jury selection. He sometimes shook his head as Petrocelli spoke and whispered to his lawyers.
Some of the victims' relatives sat sobbing in the spectators' gallery.
In his opening statement, Petrocelli alleged that Simpson killed Goldman to eliminate a witness to an earlier fatal attack on Simpson's ex-wife Nicole.
Petrocelli portrayed Goldman as a hero who "might have run" but instead stayed to face down the killer outside Nicole Brown Simpson's townhouse in Brentwood, a Los Angeles suburb.
He said Goldman was doing a favour for his friend -- returning a pair of glasses from the restaurant where he worked -- "only to come upon her vengeful killer."
"In the last furious moments of his life, Ron Goldman saw through his eyes the man who killed his friend Nicole and took his young life away, the man who sits in this courtroom," Petrocelli said.

Petrocelli also promised to present evidence in two areas that jurors in the criminal trial never heard about -- the infamous freeway chase that led to Simpson's arrest and the note he left behind suggesting he was contemplating suicide.
In terms of its racial breakdown, the mostly white jury that began hearing the case on Wednesday bears little resemblance to the mostly black panel that acquitted Simpson in his criminal trial.
Another major difference is the absence of the courtroom camera that made the last trial an international media event.

Superior Court Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki has banned cameras and microphones from the court, and outside the court he has imposed a sweeping "gag order" that so far has kept attorneys from battling one another with sound bites.

Camera crews swarmed outside the Santa Monica courthouse on Wednesday, and a handful of demonstrators and publicity seekers turned out. But it was a far more subdued scene than the media frenzy that surrounded Simpson's first trial.
One clear sign of calmer times: a scaled-down media encampment, dubbed "Camp O.J. By the Sea," built in the parking area across the street.

Simpson never took the witness stand during the last trial but he will be forced to testify in civil court. He cannot be punished with jail time but he could be forced to pay millions in damages if found "liable" for the murders.

Unlike the criminal trial, which required "proof beyond a reasonable doubt," the plaintiffs in the civil trial will prevail if they can prove there is a 50.1 percent probability - - a "preponderance of the evidence" -- that Simpson committed the murders.
And the verdict need not be unanimous -- only nine of the 12 jurors' votes are required for a judgment for or against Simpson.
